title: SLO-brokered Capacity Harmonics: Draft PRD
body:
Summary:

This document proposes a SLO-brokered capacity allocation model (working name: Capacity Harmonics) for Redwood Dedicated. The aim is to reduce tail latency incidents and harsh tenant evictions during demand spikes by explicitly treating SLOs as first-class inputs to autoscaling and burst allocation.

Why this is different / problem statement:
- Current reserved + burst designs focus on static credits and headroom pools that are agnostic to tenant SLO shapes. When demand is highly heterogeneous, low-latency tenants suffer noisy neighbor effects or are evicted to maintain pool-wide balance.
- We need an admission and brokerage layer that translates tenant SLOs (latency p50/p95/p99, throughput budgets, business criticality) into temporary, prioritized capacity reservations and graceful degradation lanes.

Goals:
- Map tenant SLO profiles to probabilistic capacity commitments so we can prioritize resources during spikes without catastrophic evictions.
- Provide soft fallback modes with controlled fidelity degradation (e.g., quantization, batching windows, reduced concurrency) for tenants with lower SLOs instead of outright preemption.
- Keep predictable economics: expose to customers how prioritized allocations affect billing, and avoid opaque cross-tenant cost shifts.
- Integrate with existing autoscaler telemetry and the headroom credit system.

Non-goals:
- Full billing redesign. We will reason about pricing implications but not finalize billing contract language here.
- Replacing per-tenant static reservations entirely. This is an augmentation layer to existing reservations and burst credit mechanisms.

High-level design (capacity broker + harmonics):
1) Tenant SLO Profiles
   - Each tenant registers an SLO profile: primary latency quantile (p50/p95/p99), throughput envelope (e.g., tokens/sec or reqs/sec), and fidelity tolerance (high / medium / low).
   - Profiles default to conservative values for existing tenants; new customers complete a brief onboarding questionnaire.

2) SLO Broker: continuous market-maker
   - The broker consumes cluster telemetry (GPU occupancy, queue lengths, latency per model variant) and tenant SLOs, and periodically computes a harmonic allocation: a time-varying vector of capacity commitments and degradation plans across tenants.
   - Harmonics is intentionally probabilistic: instead of binary reserve/no-reserve, the broker outputs p(commit) per tenant per short time window (e.g., 1m). Higher criticality/SLO -> higher p(commit) and higher priority in preemption ordering.

3) Admission & Fast-path Allocation
   - Incoming requests consult the broker for admission class. Classes: guaranteed, best-effort-high, best-effort-low.
   - Guaranteed: routes to dedicated reserved lanes; minimal batching, KV-cache pinned; preemption avoided.
   - Best-effort-high: may be temporarily placed into pooled lanes but with expedited warmup and higher chance of warm-pool recall.
   - Best-effort-low: eligible for fidelity degradation (quantization, increased batching, delayed KV recall).

4) Graceful Fidelity Degradation Lanes
   - For best-effort-low tenants the broker can activate a pre-configured degradation plan: apply a lighter-weight model variant (int8), increase batch window up to configured max_latency, or switch to cached prefix responses for repeated prompts.
   - Degradation plans are reversible and must include correctness guards and quality monitoring (see monitoring section).

5) Soft Preemption & Eviction Ordering
   - If capacity is exhausted, eviction uses broker priorities rather than pure tenure or FIFO. Eviction ordering factors: (1) probability of commitment, (2) SLO criticality, (3) economic tier (reserved commit size), (4) degradation headroom.
   - Eviction is performed with a staged handshake: 1) try degrade plan, 2) reduce concurrency, 3) nudge to pooled fallback model variant, 4) evict. Each handshake step is instrumented and auditable.

6) Economic primitives & transparency
   - Every temporary allocation has metadata: estimated token-seconds, expected latency improvement, and a short note on how it impacts billing (e.g., fallback model cost delta). This is surfaced in Console and invoices.

Integration points:
- Autoscaler: broker emits signals that bias autoscaler decisions (e.g., recommend warm-pool size, recommended fractional headroom per pool).
- Routing: per-request admission requires a low-latency lookup (redis-backed feature store or local cache in edge-router).
- Serving runtime: must support on-the-fly degradation toggles (model variant switch, quantization toggles, batching window controls).
- Console/Optimize: show per-tenant SLO burn rate and simulated outcomes for proposed broker policies.

Observability & Safety:
- Metrics: per-tenant p50/p95/p99 (observed), broker-commit-probability over time, degradation-activation-count, eviction-lag, eviction-step durations, quality regression alerts tied to eval prompt sets.
- Playbooks: set of operators steps when broker signals > X evictions in Y minutes (circuit-breaker: pause new ad-hoc degradations, escalate to SRE/product).
- Canary & guardrails: any degradation policy must pass canary quality checks using a small prompt set before rollout to all requests for that tenant.

Acceptance Criteria / Success Metrics (initial):
- Reduce high-priority tenant p99 latency tail incidents by >= 30% during correlated spikes in production clusters (first 90 days after pilot).
- Reduce forced full-evictions by 50% vs baseline where only static burst credits existed.
- No more than 0.5% of requests hit a degradation plan that triggers a quality-regression alert in the first month.

Operational plan & rollout:
- Phase 0 (simulation, 2–4 weeks): run the broker as a simulator against historical traces (we have clusters-of-interest traces in capacity-sim repo). Evaluate fairness and cost outcomes.
- Phase 1 (pilot, 6–8 weeks): enable read-only broker signals and surface recommendations in Console for two pilot tenants. No automated preemption.
- Phase 2 (kicked, 8–12 weeks): allow broker to advise autoscaler and routing for a small set of tenants (instrumented). Start small degradations only after canary checks.
- Phase 3 (wider rollout): expand to all dedicated pools with opt-in for default customers. Offer an "SLO-brokered" product tier.

Open questions & design tradeoffs:
- How fine-grained should commitment windows be? 1m windows reduce risk but increase churn; 5s windows are responsive but noisy.
- Billing implications: do we bill degraded requests at lower rate, or keep existing per-token model and surface credits? Need legal and finance input.
- Complexity: broker introduces probability and non-determinism into allocation. We need deterministic fallback logic for debugging.

Appendix A — Simulation notes (short):
- Ran a 48h trace (mixed real customer workloads) with toy broker that prioritized p95-sensitive tenants. Results: p99 tail reduced 28% for top-critical tenants but average pooled latency increased 6% during extreme spike windows. We need to tune aggregation windows and incorporate economic throttles. Link to sim: https://github.com/redwood-inference/capacity-sim/pull/17

Appendix B — UX sketches (what Console needs):
- SLO profile editor (form + suggested defaults)
- "What-if" simulator: slider for spike magnitude + predicted p99 for each tenant
- Event timeline showing degradations and broker decisions

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Product: finalize SLO profile schema and default fidelity tiers (owner: Nina).
- Engineering: prototype broker simple policy (owner: Marcus) and attach to existing autoscaler telemetry.
- Research: design a small prompt set per tenant to use as canary evals for degradations (owner: Evelyn).

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This is intentionally a lightweight concept PRD to seed design conversations. Lots of parallels to existing burst-credit ideas but the key shift is treating SLOs as weight in allocation decisions rather than only as a post-hoc SLA metric.
- If this seems directionally OK, next doc should be a single-page API contract and an autoscaler signal spec.

-- Nina
